content:
This topic has been discussed here, without a clear conclusion. It's well known that the underlying calculus of Lean is equivalent to ZFC+countable inaccessible cardinals (as we almost always use Lean with Choice and hence LEM). Some mathematicians may still feel uneasy working with a theory of a consistency strength stronger than that of ZFC, and to know if a proof in Lean is within the power of ZFC may be of interest for some. Further, what segment of Lean is equivalent to ZFC is itself an interesting metamathematical topic.

The main obstacle to a clear relation between ZFC and type theory appears to be Axiom of Replacement: Replacement works for every definable function in first order logic (and not just set theoretic functions), and therefore, intuitively, gives us a way to look at the structure of the set theoretic universe "from the outside". This intuition, translated naively to type theory, involves functions of type Type->Type, and hence inevitably motivates inclusions of type universe into the calculus - and yet once this is done, a model of ZFC can be constructed in the type theory, and the resulting type theoretic calculus is now stronger than ZFC. I remember Mario Carneiro once called this the fence post error problem.

Indeed HOL has a natural set theoretic correspondence, namely, bounded Zermelo set theory i.e. MacLane set theory, which famously lacks full Replacement.

There are ways to cut out unwanted functionalities in a type theory, resulting in a weaker calculus. A trivial example is to replace x:Type by "x Type" to say that x is a (well formed) type. A slightly less trivial example is, if we want to have a dependent typed HOL, we can introduce a separate tier of types to type type constructors, written as a∶ Πx∶A. tp, besides the Πx∶A.B types in Type 0.

I'm wondering whether it is possible to impose constraints to Lean's calculus and allow Type to (say) appear only on the right side of colon, resulting in a typed lambda calculus that's equiconsistent (equi-interpretable, actually) with ZFC, and, if possible, let (a version of) Lean's kernel to report if a proof is within the power of ZFC.

Understandably this may not be a priority of the community, especially given that many working mathematicians perhaps now think ZFC+countable inaccessible cardinals is the right foundation, considering all the category theoretic constructions we have. Still it may be an interesting metamathematical question on its own.

We definitely need more people in the foundations to go beyond the tooling and ask questions like these. People like me always want to get deeper understanding like this but typically are drained of energy to investigate on their own after a day of tool use for some domain-specific objective. Keep us in touch with further findings here or later on if possible!
I have a guess that "if a proposition can be proved in Lean with no quantification on Type 0 and higher in its subterms, then it is also provable in ZFC". Is that true?

Dexin Zhang said:

I have a guess that "if a proposition can be proved in Lean with no quantification on Type 0 and higher in its subterms, then it is also provable in ZFC". Is that true?

ZFC is FOL theory + choice , with axioms on the object “set” right ? It does not allow impredicativity and is always using “set” afaik , so that universe thing sounds right . But ultimately whatever you choose to encode FoL logic + axioms about set + choice , you would need to have your sets be in the same universe ? I just don’t think that’s enough on its own because you can have SOL(more than / different to vanilla choice ) and have them in the same universe too. Lots of different FOL axiomatic set theories out there similar to ZFC with various deviations.

Overall though ZFC and results based on it have been encoded in Lean before , to go backwards would I guess need some object in one universe along with provably only ZFC axioms involved.

Dexin Zhang said:

I have a guess that "if a proposition can be proved in Lean with no quantification on Type 0 and higher in its subterms, then it is also provable in ZFC". Is that true?

No. Lean can prove Con(ZFC), which has the form ∀ n : ℕ, f x = 0 where f : ℕ → ℕ is a primitive recursive function (that you could write down explicitly), but ZFC cannot prove Con(ZFC) (unless ZFC is inconsistent, of course).
